title: Don't Be A Lawyer, ChatGPT — Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000 Ep. 10, with Kendra Albert
pub: Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000 (DAIR Institute) — Ep. 10, recorded live on Twitch 3 March 2023, podcast edition published 16 August 2023
author: Emily M. Bender · Alex Hanna · Kendra Albert

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Albert reinforces the cluster’s competence paradox by arguing that reviewing AI output is not simply an extension of ordinary legal editing: AI can introduce unexpected fabrications that established review habits may not catch. They also add client interviewing and connection as an underemphasised capability that training and AI-enabled workflows should preserve, though they do not address the cluster’s proposed simulations or staffing effects.
qs: KENDRA ALBERT: And I say this as someone who teaches people how to practice law and so I spent a lot of time correcting or working with students to make sure their work like hits a standard that we would hand to clients, but I've never had a student produce a complaint that had the name of a court that didn't exist.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source strongly supports the cluster’s proposition that text-generation performance on bounded proxies does not establish general legal competence. It reinforces the need for selective, human-led deployment by stressing contextual and relational legal skills, unfamiliar verification burdens, confidentiality risks, and users’ unequal ability to assess plausible-looking outputs. Its stronger scepticism about generative AI for access to justice remains consistent with the cluster’s cautious, outcome-focused treatment.

kp.k: Bar-exam performance does not establish practical legal competence
kp.d: Albert considers eventual LLM bar-exam success believable because, in their assessment, the exam rewards memorisation and plausible legal language rather than the diverse skills of practice. Bender frames this as poor construct validity. Albert cites mediation and negotiation as activities for which memorised rules may be irrelevant, and regards expense, discrimination and gatekeeping as stronger criticisms of the exam than machine performance.
qs: I actually totally find it believable that a large language model could pass the bar exam, because the bar exam is a terrible measure of people's ability to practice law.
there's not one way to be a good lawyer right there's so many different things that lawyers do
if you're relying on the memorization you did for the bar exam in order to practice law like you are probably doing a bad job right.

kp.k: The discussed study did not demonstrate bar-exam passage
kp.d: Discussing reporting on GPT-3.5, Albert stresses that, as of the live recording on 3 March 2023, the study had not demonstrated passage and tested only multiple-choice questions, not essays or the performance test. GPT-4 passage was a prediction, not a reported finding. Hanna reports that evidence and torts reached an average passing rate; Albert explicitly labels their explanation of evidence performance through closer word–rule associations as speculation.
qs: part of the reason they're talking about 'GPT-4 and comparable models might be able to pass the exam very soon' is because they didn't manage to get it to pass the exam.
And also they only tested it on part of the of the bar exam, the the multiple choice version.
That's a great question and I'm going to speculate wildly.

kp.k: Top-two-answer scoring exaggerates the significance of benchmark results
kp.d: Bender criticises a graph that supplements first-choice performance with results allowing two answers per four-choice question. Albert argues that MBE questions often contain two implausible and two plausible options, so narrowing answers to two is not especially informative. Bender asks what human performance would look like under the same scoring arrangement and rejects equating even genuine exam passage with becoming a lawyer.
qs: They felt the need to include well how well would it have done if we let it pick two answers on each question.
there's usually two like often two very wrong answers and two plausible answers.
Be interesting to see what the what the human score is on that.

kp.k: Legal-data access may concentrate AI production among incumbents
kp.d: Responding to Sasha Rao's Daily Journal claim that AI can read the entire corpus of law, Albert questions both what that corpus includes and how developers could obtain it. They distinguish US case law from the entirety of law, describe costly legal search, and argue conditionally that comprehensive training could concentrate production among existing providers with access to legal information. This is a structural argument, not evidence of observed market concentration.
qs: it's actually really difficult to get a hold of the corpus of law.
U.S. case law even in the United States does not constitute the entire corpus of law
would suggest this huge centralization of the ability to produce these tools by you know existing legal providers that already have access to this information for free

kp.k: Document-centred automation claims misrepresent much legal practice
kp.d: Albert argues that Rao's assumption that relevant facts are already contained in documents reflects a narrow, business-law-oriented conception of practice. Criminal representation may require witness interviews and investigation rather than merely processing an existing document collection. Later, Albert emphasises client interviewing and connection as important skills omitted from document-generation narratives.
qs: the idea that the corpus of facts that's relevant to uh the law or a case is already pulled into documents.
there are very few areas of law right where actually you know your entire corpus of facts that's going to be relevant is going to be like nicely kind of cabined into a set of legal documents
the thing that's important in practicing law is sort of the ability to kind of interview and connect with a client

kp.k: Text manipulation is not equivalent to legal understanding
kp.d: Bender challenges the Daily Journal article's move from language-based information to supposedly ready understanding. They distinguish computer input processing from human reading and argue that selecting evidence and constructing narratives remain substantive questions. Even treating such work as supervised text manipulation would require testing performance, comparing training-data production costs with doing the legal work directly, and addressing changing circumstances.
qs: we talk about humans reading and it is not the same thing.
I think that that is better phrased as 'readily manipulated because it is based on language,'
is the production of that training data actually cheaper than just going ahead and doing the lawyering yourself?
that training set is always going to be locked at some point in the past and not ready to deal with changing circumstances.

kp.k: Client-data training creates confidentiality and disclosure risks
kp.d: Albert uses a student's request to use Grammarly on clinic work to explain why client obligations extend beyond whether a tool functions well. They argue that vendors have incentives to train on submitted contracts, precedents and memoranda, while models can reproduce training data. Disclosure to other firms or deliberately crafted opposing-side queries is presented as a potential risk, not an observed legal-client incident. Albert recommends considering these consequences and obtaining robust security guarantees before submitting client information.
qs: we're practicing law for real clients. so we have ethical obligations with regard to them.
LLMs will just straight up produce training data right?
you could craft queries to try and get that stuff that they've written out of it.
you should not be putting client information into this stuff until you've actually thought about what it means, if it might get produced to other council.

kp.k: Professional ethics provide guardrails, but enforcement remains uncertain
kp.d: Albert distinguishes criticism of state bars from recognition that ethical practice rules constrain harmful client-facing tools. They suggest law has guardrails that some other fields lack, while explicitly leaving open whether bars will enforce them. The discussion does not identify particular professional-rule provisions.
qs: there are some constraints around usages of tools that are going to be bad or harmful to your clients.
whether we see bars enforcing them is another question

kp.k: A generated complaint illustrates plausible form masking factual error
kp.d: Albert examines Andrew M. Perlman's preprint, which reports generating most of its text through ChatGPT in about an hour without human editing. A sample Massachusetts complaint names the Court of Common Pleas; Albert states that this court has not existed there since 1860 and criticises the paper for not flagging the error. This is a specific inspected example of unreliable output and inadequate verification, not a measured hallucination rate.
qs: ChatGPTgenerated the rest of the text with no human editing.
The Court of Common Pleas is not a court that currently exists in Massachusetts.
In fact it's a court that has not existed in Massachusetts since 1860.
there's no indication in this article that that's true.

kp.k: Credence-good characteristics amplify risks for unrepresented clients
kp.d: Albert describes legal services as a credence good: clients, particularly nonlawyers, struggle to assess quality and may use legal-looking formatting and vocabulary as proxies. Plausible generated documents therefore pose particular risks for low-income people without access to lawyers. Hanna describes potentially devastating consequences for someone relying on generated documents without counsel; this is a prospective harm argument, not a documented outcome in the episode.
qs: legal services is what's called a credence good.
it's especially not easy for people who are not lawyers to evaluate.
Does it look like law stuff?
they're not in an effective position to evaluate these kinds of things even already even pre you know GPT generation of documents.

kp.k: The justice gap does not establish AI's suitability
kp.d: Bender rejects the argument that unaffordable legal representation makes ChatGPT an acceptable substitute. Albert points instead to easier pro se forms, demystification of legal processes, expanded nonlawyer qualifications and reduced attorney student debt as human interventions they believe can improve availability or lower costs. Albert tentatively identifies Washington State as an example of a 'paralegal plus' certification; the episode supplies no comparative effectiveness estimates.
qs: You've identified a problem, access to legal services is too expensive, that doesn't make this technology the solution.
forms that are easier for folks to like fill out
I think it's Washington State has basically sort of like a paralegal plus certification for tasks that where it actually doesn't make sense to have an attorney do it.
decreasing student loans for attorneys decreases the price for uh you know like pay you know--uh decreases the price for legal services.

kp.k: AI-draft verification differs from reviewing junior lawyers' work
kp.d: Responding to Perlman's prediction that lawyers may soon generate complex first drafts incorporating firm style and knowledge, Albert challenges the assumption that correction uses familiar supervisory skills. Drawing on teaching and reviewing student work, they argue that an invented court name is outside ordinary expectations of a human draft, making AI verification qualitatively different. Hanna adds that substituting correction for scaffolded knowledge formation reflects a flawed account of learning.
qs: the idea that generating a first draft with one of these tools and then correcting it is a similar skill to one that lawyers already have is just totally bonkers to me.
I've never had a student produce a complaint that had the name of a court that didn't exist.
that's not a thing that lawyers check for
while you should be scaffolding knowledge instead you're thinking about um knowledge in education as being a corrective

kp.k: Fabricated precedent creates additional checking work
kp.d: Albert reads Ann Lipton's account of someone using ChatGPT to suggest purported shareholder cases and settlement amounts that never existed. Bender characterises this as creating work rather than providing assistance. The evidence is a quoted third-party anecdote, not a court sanctions incident or systematic study.
qs: someone on Twitter used jet--ChatGPT to direct me to purportedly precedent cases where shareholders have brought particular claims and settled for particular amounts. None of it was real; the cases never happened.
Making extra work rather than helping people.

kp.k: Cross-domain examples show costs imposed on nonusers
kp.d: The hosts discuss a reported fabricated Signal integration that directed a user to journalist Dave Lee's number, a Vanderbilt message after the Michigan shootings using ChatGPT, and Clarkesworld closing submissions after AI-generated story spam. They use these anecdotes to illustrate bystander disruption, inappropriate outsourcing of emotionally meaningful communication, and increased review burdens that can undermine inclusive access to publishing. Bender explicitly leaves uncertain whether Lee's number came from training data or number generation.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kendra Albert distinguishes plausible AI success on bar examinations from legal competence, and identifies limitations and risks in AI drafting, verification, confidentiality, access to justice and market concentration.
pts.d: Albert makes six principal claims. (1) A language model could plausibly pass bar-examination components, including essays, because the examination rewards memorization and legal-sounding expression rather than adequately measuring practice skills; the study discussed had not demonstrated a passing result. Albert also tentatively predicts that future model success might make some examination defenders more receptive to criticism of the bar. (2) Training on an assumed complete legal corpus would not by itself establish legal competence. Difficulty obtaining legal materials could concentrate tool development among incumbent legal-information providers with existing access. Moreover, document-contained facts represent only a narrow conception of practice: criminal representation, for example, can require interviewing witnesses and investigation. (3) Using client work to train tools could expose confidential or privileged information through reproduced training material, potentially including extraction by opposing counsel. (4) AI-generated drafts can introduce errors outside lawyers' usual expectations, making verification materially different from editing a student's or lawyer's first draft. (5) Plausible-looking but incorrect legal documents pose particular risks to low-income people unable to obtain counsel or assess quality; Albert does not treat the existence of unmet legal need as evidence that generated documents solve it, and instead points to forms, expanded nonlawyer qualifications and reduced attorney debt as alternative interventions. (6) Professional ethical rules provide some constraints on harmful AI use, although enforcement is uncertain. These are Albert's positions, not endorsements of the optimistic claims by Sasha Rao or Andrew Perlman that the episode critiques.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Albert relies on professional and teaching experience, a limited bar-examination study discussed secondhand, and inspection of a generated complaint; broader market and confidentiality consequences are reasoned risks rather than measured outcomes.
pts.d: For the examination claim, Albert cites having taken the bar three times, including failing California on the first attempt, and explains the mismatch between memorization and work such as mediation or negotiation. The discussed GPT-3.5 study tested multiple-choice questions, not essays or the performance test. Albert criticizes treating the model's top two answers as particularly informative because questions often contain two implausible and two plausible options. Their explanation for stronger evidence-question performance is explicitly labeled speculation, not a finding. For drafting and verification, Albert inspected the complaint reproduced in Perlman's paper: it named a Massachusetts Court of Common Pleas, which Albert says had not existed there since 1860, without the paper flagging the error. Albert contrasts this with their experience supervising law students, none of whom had produced that type of error. This is a concrete illustrative example, not a measured hallucination rate or court-sanctions incident. For confidentiality, Albert cites training-data reproduction associated with tools such as Copilot and a clinic student's request to use Grammarly; no actual disclosure of that clinic's client information or successful opposing-counsel extraction is reported. The concentration claim rests on Albert's account of restricted and expensive legal research access, not market-share data. The access-to-justice concern rests on the characterization of legal services as a credence good and the difficulty nonlawyers face in assessing quality. No quantified productivity, displacement, pricing or client-outcome study is offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims reflect the live discussion on 3 March 2023; future examination success and downstream harms are conditional, with no numerical adoption or transformation deadline.
pts.d: Although the podcast edition appeared on 16 August 2023, Albert repeatedly frames examination non-passage as the situation at recording. Their suggestion that models could pass parts of the bar is prospective and is not a report of subsequent GPT-4 results. Their possible effect on bar-exam defenders is qualified by 'it could be' and 'We'll see.' Market concentration is conditional on pursuing tools trained on legal sources requiring access that relatively few actors possess. Confidentiality risks concern sharing client materials with a manufacturer, especially where inputs may become training data and robust security guarantees are absent; Albert does not establish that every legal AI deployment follows that arrangement. Verification concerns persist even under a first-draft-only, human-review workflow, rather than applying solely to autonomous legal practice. The discussion of missing facts is qualified by practice area: the document-centered vision is more characteristic of business-law settings than of all legal work. Ethical safeguards already exist, but Albert expressly separates their existence from whether bars will enforce them.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are lawyers and trainees reviewing drafts, clients whose information is supplied to tools, people lacking affordable counsel, legal-information incumbents and prospective entrants, and licensing institutions.
pts.d: Lawyers, supervising clinicians and students face unfamiliar verification demands rather than a demonstrated reduction in total work. Clients face potential disclosure of confidential information, including to opposing counsel, if their work is incorporated into reusable training data. Low-income people without high-quality representation are especially exposed to plausible legal formatting that they cannot reliably evaluate; this is an access-to-justice concern, not an enterprise cost-saving claim. Criminal defendants illustrate why lawyering cannot generally be reduced to processing an existing document collection. Incumbents with legal-information access could gain an advantage in producing specialized tools, while others face barriers to obtaining training sources. Bar candidates and examination defenders are affected by questions about what a model's test success actually demonstrates. Albert does not predict a specific staffing shape, headcount reduction, replacement rate or billing-model change.
